Issued at 124 PM CDT Thu Oct 22 2026

THIS AFTERNOON: Another beautiful afternoon across the Tri-
State area as temperatures continue to rise into the 70s. As the
SPG continues to increase surface winds are beginning to gust 
over 20 to 25 mph at times, highest along and west of the James 
River valley. Mid- lvl clouds associated with a broad increase 
in 600:500 mb RH will continue to spread northeast, through have
been thinning. Fire danger remains high in most areas west of 
I-29 so caution should be used in farm fields into the evening.

TONIGHT: Winds will remain breezy through the overnight hours, 
keeping overnight lows much warmer than normal. After midnight, 
we'll begin to see the breakout of mid-lvl clouds as warm 
advection within the 700:600 mb range increases. Short term CAMs
are coming into more consensus in the development of scattered 
high based showers after 3am, which may increase further by 
12-15Z as lift maximizes on the increased LLJ moving into SW 
Minnesota. While a very low chance, MUCAPE in the effective 
layer rises up to 200-300 J/KG indicating at least isolated 
lightning potential. Will increase POTThunder to account for the
risks.

FRIDAY: Any morning shower and isolated storm activity will 
lift into west central and central Minnesota by mid-day. 
Troughing entering the Central Rockies will further intensify 
the SPG through the day, with sustained winds of 15 to 20 mph 
developing by mid-day. Despite the SE surface flow, we're likely
to see gusts increase towards the 35 to 45 mph range by mid-day
with these gusts continuing into the very early evening hours. 
Temperatures may be a bit more uncertain Friday afternoon, 
somewhat dependent on lingering mid- lvl cloud cover. The 
warmest reading are still expected along and west of the James 
River where upper 70s to lower 80s may be possible. Greater 
temperature spreads remain over SW Minnesota where highs could 
range anywhere from the lower 70s with clouds to the upper 70s. 
Warm temperatures and strong winds will lead to elevated to near
critical fire danger. Please see separate discussion on fire 
weather risks. 

SATURDAY: A frontal boundary that remained over western South 
Dakota Friday will begin to advance eastward overnight reaching 
into the western half of the CWA by daybreak Saturday. Mid-lvl 
vorticity streaming NE along this frontal zone may lead to 
scattered high bases showers to sprinkles through the day on 
Saturday. Soundings show ceiling bases only as low as 8K ft AGL 
by Saturday afternoon, with a fair amount of dry air still 
infiltrating the sub-cloud layer in the afternoon. This should 
help keep any QPF on the low side and rain more sporadic. The 
front and clouds could have a profound impact on afternoon 
temperatures, with some guidance suggesting highs near 60 well 
behind the front, with highs closer to 75 in areas near Sioux 
City to Storm Lake and Spencer more displaced from the boundary.
This light rain opportunity will continue through Saturday 
night into Sunday morning as the surface and low-lvl boundary 
remains stalled overhead. 

SUNDAY-WEDNESDAY: A bit more uncertainty develops on Sunday, 
focused around the positioning of the surface front. Models like
the NAM, that tend to be overly strong on cold air surges 
southeast, push the front all the way towards central Iowa. The 
ECMWF on the other hand increases mid-lvl ridging through the 
Central Plains and slows the arrival of upper troughing over the
Central and Southern Rockies. This in return forces the 
boundary further northwest. The GFS splits the two solutions, 
keeping the boundary nearby and focusing more clouds and 
occasional spits of rain through the heart of the CWA. Never 
mind the solution, there may be brief lull in rainfall on Sunday
with most guidance suggesting any rain chances diminish during 
the the first two thirds of the daytime hours. 

Those rain chances increase once again Sunday night and 
continue through Monday as the upper trough over the Rockies 
begins to eject into the Plains. Increasing mid-lvl warm 
advection will assist in developing a narrow low-lvl frontal 
zone near the Tri-State area that should drive more persistent 
rain chances. More direct lift from the upper wave itself 
arrives late Monday into Monday night, though there remains 
considerable uncertainty on the track of the upper wave. 
Needless to say, probabilistic data continues to indicate high 
rain chances through the region, but indicate quite a spread on 
potential rainfall totals. Standard 25/75th QPF ranges from the 
NBM suggest anywhere from 0.50"-1.75" for most of the CWA, with 
probabilities for >1.0" greater than 60% still focused along and
west of the James River and into the Missouri River valley. 

In addition to the rain, another more direct impact from this
